title: The prince's unease
hookLine: the road cleared of the old and sick, yet the gods place an old man in his path (Buddhacarita 3)

lines: KEEP THE OLD AND SICK AWAY.
cards: Orders go out across the city. Sweep the royal road. Hang garlands.
Set out banners and flowers. And one more order, the strange one: anyone old, anyone sick, anyone suffering, keep them off the road today.
The prince has asked to see the gardens outside the walls, and the king, Shuddhodana, has said yes, on one condition. The world his son sees will have the hard parts taken out.
By the time the chariot rolls through the gate, the street is perfect. Faces at every window. Not a single bent back in sight.

teach.b: First, the crowd. People hurry to rooftops and windows to catch sight of the prince going by, and they look at him with delight. It's a parade, and for a moment the king's plan seems to work.
Second, the gap. The road has been cleared; nobody old should be there.

teach.h: THE GODS PLACE AN OLD MAN.
teach.b: So the poem says the gods of the pure abodes made one: an old man appears in the prince's path, bent over, white-haired, leaning on a stick. The wall the king built was solid. Something came through it anyway.
Third, the question. The prince turns to his charioteer and asks what this is. The charioteer answers simply: this is old age.
It takes beauty and strength and memory. This man was a child once, and grew, and this is where the years have brought him. Then the question that matters.
The answer is yes. To you, and to everyone. Fourth, the unease.
The prince is shaken to the core. He can't enjoy the gardens, and asks to turn back. The king's whole plan was about keeping things out.
The poem's answer is that some truths don't need permission.

how: Buddhist teachers return to the sights of old age, sickness and death when teaching impermanence, and the scenes are painted on temple walls and told to children in Buddhist communities.

o: an illness that strikes only the unlucky
a punishment the gods send to one man
what time brings to everyone, prince included

games.q: the first sight in the poem: tap the pairs.
p: keep the old and sick off the road
the gods of the pure abodes
place an old man in his path
asks, will this happen to me?

s: in the poem, the old man was there by chance
the road was cleared; the poem says the gods of the pure abodes made him appear.
the charioteer tells the prince age will come to him too
the prince enjoys the gardens after the sight
he is shaken and asks to turn back.

games.q: you're the charioteer. the prince points at an old man the king's orders should have kept away and asks what he is. what do you say?
o: tell him it's nothing, and drive on.
tell him plainly: this is old age, and it comes to everyone.
tell him to ask his father.
games.why: the charioteer names it plainly, and when the prince asks if it will happen to him, says yes.

practice: Turn your hands over slowly and look at them as if for the first time: the lines at the knuckles, the creases of the palm, any scar, any spot. These hands were small once, and they will change again.
Ask the prince's question quietly, without fear, will this happen to me, and keep breathing beside the honest answer.

wordCard.voice: old age. The charioteer's answer when the prince asks about the bent, white-haired man on the road: it takes beauty, strength and memory, and comes to everyone, the prince included. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: it gets through anyway. The road was cleared, and old age still found it. Day seven hundred one.

sources.ref: Buddhacarita 3 (the road cleared; the old man)
